newsitem.title: USA: Wealthy U.S. businessman freed after kidnap ordeal.
newsitem.headline: Wealthy U.S. businessman freed after kidnap ordeal.

text.p: A wealthy San Francisco businessman was freed unharmed on Tuesday after being held for eight hours by two men who kidnapped him at gunpoint from his home and demanded a $500,000 ransom, police said.
Marshall Wais, a 79-year-old steel magnate, was driven around blindfolded for hours while the kidnappers negotiated the ransom payment.
His harrowing ordeal ended when the kidnappers released him in the city's Golden Gate Park in mid-afternoon after picking up the ransom money paid by his family.
Minutes later, police, who had the kidnappers under surveillance, pounced. A police car rammed the kidnappers' van and officers arrested the two suspects and recovered the ransom money.

"We're happy to report that the victim has been returned to his family safely. We have two suspects in custody," John Willett, police deputy chief of investigations, said. "There was a ransom for half a million dollars and that money was recovered."
Local news organisations learned of the kidnapping during the day but did not report it until after Wais's release after being asked to do so by police.

Wais, the owner of Marway Steel, based in nearby Richmond, California, appeared tired but in good health when he spoke to reporters later at his multi-million-dollar home in the upscale Seacliff area overlooking San Francisco Bay.
"The San Francisco Police Department and the Federal Bureau of Investigation did one fabulous job. They got the guys, they did it right," said Wais, who is married with three adult children.

The kidnapping began early on Tuesday when two armed men pushed their way into Wais's house behind a housekeeper. Wais told reporters he was awakened by one of the men, who initially demanded $1 million. "I didn't quite have that much on me," he joked.
The men put him in a van and blindfolded him. Wais said the men did not harm him but did threaten him, telling him if there were any police around "that would be the end of me."

About two hours after he was abducted, police said, one of Wais's businesses received a telephone call demanding payment of a $500,000 ransom. That was followed by at least three other calls making demands and giving instructions.
Ryan said the callers indicated Wais's family should pay up if they wanted to see him alive again. The ransom money was provided "with the cooperation of the family," Ryan said.

Following the kidnappers' demands, the ransom money was left in a parked car, which was kept under surveillance by police, Ryan said. The kidnappers picked up the money and released Wais soon afterwards.

A police car then rammed the kidnappers' vehicle and officers arrested Michael Robison, 35, and Thomas Taylor, 64. The men, who both have criminal records, could face kidnapping and burglary charges, Ryan said.
